conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your neurology doctors. You’ve been transferred here because of the left-sided weakness you’ve been having.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started three days ago. I couldn’t lift my arm or leg on the left side. I thought it was another MS flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your MRI from the other hospital. It shows a large lesion on the right side of your brain with swelling. That could explain the weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it MS? I was treated with steroids already, but I didn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. MS usually responds to steroids. This lesion looks more like a tumor or something else. We need to get more information.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A tumor? That’s scary. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on dexamethasone to reduce brain swelling. We’ll also do a CT scan tonight to check for any bleeding or changes in the mass effect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. There’s no bleeding, but the mass is causing significant pressure and shifting the brain to the left. We’re very concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it can be. That’s why we increased your dexamethasone and started mannitol to help reduce the swelling. We’re also starting an anti-seizure medication as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. The steroids are helping—your strength is already a bit better than when you arrived. But we need to know what the lesion is. A biopsy may be necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your speech is a little more slurred today, so we’re keeping the high-dose steroids. We’re planning a stereotactic brain biopsy to get a tissue sample.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Biopsy? Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a precise procedure guided by imaging. The neurosurgeons will use a small needle to get a sample. It’s the best way to know what we’re dealing with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then we’ll know if it’s cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It could be lymphoma, a tumor, or something else. The biopsy will tell us. We’ll schedule it as soon as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today is the day of your biopsy. You’ll go to the operating room in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. How long will it take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure itself is about an hour. You’ll be under anesthesia. Afterward, you’ll go to the neuro-ICU for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when will we know the results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have preliminary results in a day or two. The final pathology will take longer. We’ll keep you updated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from surgery. The biopsy went well. The CT scan shows a small amount of air and blood in the brain, which is expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did they get enough tissue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they did. The initial report suggests it might be primary CNS lymphoma. We’re waiting for confirmation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lymphoma? In the brain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s rare but possible. It’s not related to your MS. We’ll start chemotherapy soon, once we confirm the diagnosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your strength is improving. The left facial droop is less noticeable. We’re transferring you to the regular floor today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The preliminary pathology supports primary CNS B-cell lymphoma. We’ll start methotrexate, a type of chemotherapy, in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I lose my hair?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Methotrexate can cause hair thinning, but not always complete loss. We’ll monitor for side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having pain in my right chest and back when I breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be a blood clot in your lung. We’re going to do an ultrasound of your legs to check for clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound shows a deep vein thrombosis in your left calf. That explains the chest pain. We’re starting a heparin drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I have a clot in my leg and probably in my lung?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. We can’t do a CT scan with contrast right now because of the upcoming chemotherapy, but we’ll treat it as a pulmonary embolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the heparin help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Once you’re stable, we’ll switch you to Lovenox injections you can take at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed a fever and your oxygen levels dropped. We did a chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks like healthcare-associated pneumonia. We’re starting IV antibiotics—vancomycin and cefepime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on IVs the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line so you can finish antibiotics at home. You’ll continue them for eight days total.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we start your first dose of methotrexate. It’s given through the PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How will I feel after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel tired or nauseous. We’ll give you anti-nausea medication and monitor your blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your strength continues to improve. You’re moving your left arm and leg much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fever is gone, and your oxygen levels are normal. The antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you from heparin to Lovenox injections. You’ll take those twice daily at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can give myself those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a nurse will teach you and your husband how to do it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain is likely from the pleuritic chest pain. The CT showed no issues in your belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s getting better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also managing your constipation with stool softeners and laxatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line is in place. You’ll get your antibiotics through it at the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I go after here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To an extended care facility to recover and finish antibiotics. Then you’ll come back next week for more chemotherapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. The infection markers are down, and your blood counts are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I walk a little now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with a walker. Physical therapy will help you regain strength before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medications will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue dexamethasone twice daily, Keppra for seizures, Lovenox injections, and the antibiotics for four more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ulcerative colitis meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding mesalamine for now because it can interfere with methotrexate. You’ll restart it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Next week for your second dose of methotrexate. Oncology will coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep taking your meds, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your final biopsy results are pending, but everything so far confirms CNS lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’m ready to keep fighting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. We’re here with you every step of the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I ever walk normally again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already doing better. With rehab and treatment, we expect continued improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That gives me hope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re optimistic too. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’ll support you all the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well, and we’ll see you next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming your discharge time. You’re all set to go. We’ll follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mrs. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your neurology team members. You're here today for your second dose of methotrexate for your primary CNS lymphoma. How have you been feeling since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been doing okay overall. I’ve been at the rehab center and working on my strength. But I’ve noticed this numbness and tingling in my right foot for about a week now. It feels like it’s fallen asleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is the numbness constant? Does it go up your leg at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started just in the foot, but over the last couple of days, the tingling has moved up a bit—now it’s going up the outside of my leg, maybe halfway to my thigh. It’s not severe, but it’s bothersome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting me know. Given your history of CNS lymphoma and MS, we want to make sure this isn’t related to nerve involvement from the cancer spreading. We’ll start with an ultrasound to rule out a blood clot, since you’re also on blood thinners for your DVT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I wasn’t sure if it was just my MS acting up again or something more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point—MS can definitely cause these kinds of symptoms. But because of your lymphoma, we have to be extra cautious and rule out other causes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the results of your leg ultrasound. Good news—it shows no sign of a deep vein thrombosis. Your veins look normal with good blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s not a clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not a clot. But since the pain is moving up your leg, we’d like to do an MRI of your spine to make sure there’s no involvement of the spinal nerves by the lymphoma—specifically, we’re looking for something called leptomeningeal spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that common with my type of lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not common, but it can happen. The MRI will help us be sure. We’ll schedule it for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today you’ll be getting your second dose of methotrexate. We’ll give it through your PICC line, and you’ll also get leucovorin, sodium bicarbonate, and dexamethasone to protect your body from side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel different after the infusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people tolerate it well. Some feel tired or have mild nausea, but we’ll monitor you closely. The dexamethasone also helps with brain swelling and might improve your energy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great with the methotrexate infusion. No complications so far. We’ll keep an eye on your labs over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m glad that’s done. Any update on the MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The spine MRI is back. I have good news—there’s no sign of lymphoma spreading to the spinal fluid or nerves. No leptomeningeal enhancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s such a relief. So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI did show some mild degenerative changes in your lower back, especially at L3-4, where there’s some narrowing near a nerve root. But it’s not pressing on anything. Given your history of MS, it’s possible this is a new flare of your MS affecting sensation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it could be MS, not the cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s actually the more likely explanation now that we’ve ruled out serious causes. We’d like to start you on gabapentin to help with the nerve pain and see if it improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve heard of that. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe and commonly used for neuropathic pain. We’ll start low and go slow to avoid dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I also want to talk about your liver tests. Your AST and ALT are elevated—higher than when you were last here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, yes. Methotrexate can affect the liver, and so can Keppra, which you’re on for seizure prevention. We’ve increased your leucovorin and IV fluids with sodium bicarbonate to help clear the methotrexate faster and protect your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we expect it will. We’ll keep monitoring, and you’ll take leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate by mouth for three more days after discharge. Your oncologist will check your liver enzymes in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed my dexamethasone was changed from twice a day to once a day. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s part of tapering down. You’ve been on it for a while, and we want to reduce side effects like high blood sugar or mood changes. Since your brain swelling is under control, we can safely lower the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And what about my stomach medicine? I saw we switched from omeprazole to ranitidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good catch. Ranitidine doesn’t interact with methotrexate like omeprazole can, so it’s safer during chemo. It still protects your stomach, especially since you’re on steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your methotrexate level has dropped to a safe range. That means your body is clearing it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. It means the leucovorin and hydration are working. Your liver numbers are still high, but we’ll keep following them as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling ready to go home. Will I need to come back soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in two weeks. That’s when you’ll get your third dose of methotrexate, and you’ll also have a port placed by interventional radiology for easier access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the port help with the infusions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’ll make things much smoother and reduce the need for repeated PICC lines. But you’ll need to hold your Lovenox injections the night before and the morning of that admission to reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I should keep taking the new gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice a day. If it helps, great. If not, your neurologist can adjust it. Also, keep taking your other meds like Advair, Singulair, and the calcium and vitamin D.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw on the discharge papers that they’re checking for hepatitis C. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s just a routine check. The result is pending, but if it’s positive, it’s important to know before continuing methotrexate, since it can affect the liver more in that case. We’ll follow up with your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Everything looks good for discharge. Your neurologic exam is stable, your vitals are normal, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve been looking forward to going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with prescriptions for gabapentin, ranitidine, and a few days of leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate. Stop the Dilaudid and omeprazole—we don’t need them anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll see the oncologist soon for the lab follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll call you about your liver tests. And we’ll see you back here in two weeks for the port and next chemo dose. Keep in touch with your husband and let us know if anything changes—like new weakness, severe pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well, and we’re here to support you. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this hospital stay. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m okay. A little anxious. This is my third chemo cycle, right? I just want to get through it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re doing great so far. We’re here to make sure everything goes smoothly. We’ll start with some labs and get you ready for your methotrexate tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My foot’s still hurting—same as last time. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re watching that closely. Last time, the ultrasound and MRI didn’t show a blood clot or nerve compression. We think it’s related to either your MS or the chemo. We’ll keep you on gabapentin and adjust it if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lip—I’ve got this sore on the right side. It’s new. Could that be a cold sore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a herpes simplex lesion. Since you’re on steroids, which can weaken your immune response, we’re going to start you on acyclovir to prevent it from spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve had cold sores before, but not during chemo. Is that common?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can happen, especially with steroids. That’s why we’re being proactive. The acyclovir will help keep it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my liver numbers were high last time. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that. The transaminitis is likely due to the methotrexate. Your hepatitis tests came back negative, so it’s not an infection. We’ll keep an eye on it and support your liver with hydration and bicarbonate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’m still on the blood thinner for the clot from last cycle?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, enoxaparin twice a day. We’re continuing that to prevent another clot. You’re also getting it as extra protection during this hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another PE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing everything we can to prevent that. Now, tomorrow morning, you’ll have a port placed before chemo. It’ll make the infusion easier and safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the procedure in my neck? I saw it on the schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a small catheter will be placed in your right internal jugular vein, with the port under the skin on your chest. It’s done with ultrasound and X-ray guidance. Very safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation and local numbing. Most patients feel pressure but not pain. Afterward, you might have some soreness, but we’ll manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And the chemo—same dose as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, high-dose methotrexate at 8 grams per square meter. We’ll give you IV bicarbonate before and during to protect your kidneys and help clear the drug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We start it 24 hours after chemo and give it every six hours to rescue your healthy cells. We’ll check your methotrexate levels daily to guide how long you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Ready for your port placement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: As ready as I’ll ever be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The port was placed successfully. The tip is in the right spot, and it’s ready to use. You did great. Any discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little sore where they put it. Nothing bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep an eye on it. Now, we’ll start your methotrexate infusion this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your chemo now. We’ve given IV bicarbonate to alkalinize your urine. This helps the methotrexate leave your body safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will the infusion take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About four hours. You’ll stay hydrated with IV fluids containing bicarbonate. We’ll check your urine pH regularly to make sure it stays above 7.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You tolerated it well. No nausea or reactions. We’ll start leucovorin tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My foot’s aching more today. Can we do anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can increase your gabapentin from 300 mg twice a day to 400 mg three times a day. We’ll also keep oxycodone available for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, let’s try that. And my lip sore—is the acyclovir helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should reduce healing time and prevent new outbreaks. Keep it clean and let us know if it worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level this morning is 0.44, which is low and expected. We’ll continue leucovorin every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? Last time I had to stay longer because of high levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This level is actually good. It means the drug is clearing well. You won’t need extra leucovorin or bicarbonate beyond what we’re already giving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about my liver tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ALT and AST are still elevated but coming down—from 199 to 155 and 112 to 60. This suggests improvement. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a lumbar puncture tomorrow to check your spinal fluid for any lymphoma cells. It’s a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt? I’ve never had one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get numbing medicine. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. It takes about 20 minutes. We do it to make sure the lymphoma hasn’t spread to the spinal fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it has?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d treat it with intrathecal chemotherapy. But based on your symptoms and scans, it’s unlikely. This is just being thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lumbar puncture went well. You did great. The fluid will be tested, but results will take a few days. For now, we’re discharging you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? I feel okay. But what about the results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you with the results. You’re stable, your methotrexate is cleared, and your pain is managed. You’ll follow up with oncology in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds—anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart it today. We held it because of bleeding risk, but it’s safe now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Keep taking your meds, watch for nausea, and call if anything changes. See you next month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we refilled your lorazepam prescription in case you need it for nausea or anxiety at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. I’ll keep it on hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your depression—how have you been feeling emotionally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I think. A bit anxious around treatments, but citalopram helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Don’t hesitate to talk to your psychiatrist if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I’ve got support at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Take care of yourself. We’ll see you in four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be ready. Thank you, Doctor.
